front: What does omnipotent mean?
back: All-powerful — there is nothing God cannot do.

front: What does omnibenevolent mean?
back: All-loving.

front: What does it mean to say God is just?
back: God is fair and brings about what is right — rewarding good and punishing evil.

front: Give a Bible quotation showing God is omnipotent.
back: "Nothing is impossible with God" (Luke 1:37).

front: Give a Bible quotation showing God is loving.
back: "For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son" (John 3:16). Or "God is love" (1 John 4:8).

front: What is the problem of evil and suffering?
back: If God is all-loving he would want to stop suffering; if all-powerful he could stop it. Yet suffering exists — so how can God be both?

front: What is a theodicy?
back: A religious response to the problem of evil and suffering — a defence of God's goodness.

front: Name three Christian theodicies and who is linked to each.
back: Free will (Augustine / Plantinga), original sin (Augustine), vale of soul-making (John Hick).
items: Free will — God gave humans freedom; most suffering comes from misusing it
Original sin — evil entered the world through Adam and Eve's disobedience
Vale of soul-making — suffering helps us grow and become better people

front: Explain one way belief that God is loving influences Christians today.
back: They try to love others as God loves them — e.g. helping the poor through charities — because "Love is patient, love is kind" (1 Corinthians 13:4) and God's love is the example.

front: What is the Trinity?
back: The belief in one God in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

front: What three statements about the Trinity are all true at once?
back: There is one God; each person is fully God; the persons are not the same as each other.
items: Each person of the Trinity is fully God
The persons are not the same as each other

front: At which event in Jesus' life are all three persons of the Trinity present?
back: His baptism: the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father's voice says "You are my Son, whom I love" (Mark 1:11).

front: What is the role of the Holy Spirit?
back: The unseen power of God at work in the world — guiding, strengthening and sustaining believers.

front: What does monotheistic mean?
back: Believing in only one God.

front: What does Genesis 1:1-3 teach about creation?
back: God created everything, creation is good, and the Spirit of God was present ("hovering over the waters").

front: What does John 1:1-3 add to the Christian understanding of creation?
back: The Word — Jesus, God the Son — was there and "through him all things were made". So all three persons of the Trinity were involved.

front: Literal vs non-literal readings of Genesis.
back: Literalists (creationists) take it as an exact account — six days, a young earth. Most Christians read it as religious truth (God made the world and it is good), not science, so it fits with the Big Bang and evolution.

front: What does ex nihilo mean?
back: Out of nothing — God created the universe from nothing.

front: What does the Apostles' Creed say about the afterlife?
back: Jesus "will come to judge the living and the dead"; Christians believe in "the resurrection of the body, and the life everlasting".

front: What does the Parable of the Sheep and the Goats teach?
back: People will be judged on how they treated those in need — feeding the hungry, welcoming strangers, clothing the naked, visiting the sick and prisoners. The sheep go to heaven, the goats to hell (Matthew 25).

front: Two Christian views of resurrection.
back: Physical: the body is raised and transformed (Catholic view). Spiritual: the soul is raised — "it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Corinthians 15:44).

front: Traditional vs modern views of hell.
back: Traditional: a place of eternal fire and punishment ("eternal fire", Matthew 25:41). Modern: a state of being cut off from God for ever.

front: What is universalism?
back: The belief that a loving God will in the end save everyone.

front: How does Jesus describe heaven in John 14:2?
back: "My Father's house has many rooms."

front: What is the incarnation?
back: God becoming flesh — God the Son becoming human in Jesus, fully God and fully human.

front: Give a quotation about the incarnation.
back: "The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us" (John 1:14).

front: What did Jesus answer at his trial when asked if he was the Son of the Blessed One?
back: "I am" (Mark 14:62) — and he was accused of blasphemy.

front: What did Jesus say on the cross about those crucifying him?
back: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34).

front: What did the Roman centurion say at the crucifixion?
back: "Surely this man was the Son of God!" (Mark 15:39).

front: What is the ascension?
back: Jesus returning to God the Father in heaven, 40 days after the resurrection.

front: Why is the resurrection so important to Christians?
back: It shows Jesus defeated death and promises believers eternal life. "If Christ has not been raised… your faith is futile" (1 Corinthians 15:14–17).

front: Who is named as finding the empty tomb in all four gospels?
back: Mary Magdalene.

front: What is sin?
back: Any thought or action that separates humans from God, or goes against God's law.

front: What is original sin?
back: The inbuilt tendency to do wrong that all humans are born with, inherited from Adam and Eve's disobedience in the Garden of Eden.

front: Who committed the first (original) sin?
back: Adam and Eve, by eating fruit from the forbidden tree (Genesis 3).

front: What is salvation?
back: Being saved from sin and its consequences, and admitted to heaven.

front: What is grace?
back: God's love and help, freely given — it does not have to be earned.

front: Salvation through works vs through grace.
back: Works / law: faith must be shown by obeying God and doing good — "faith… not accompanied by action is dead" (James 2:17). Grace: salvation is a free gift through faith in Jesus — "by grace you have been saved, through faith… not by works" (Ephesians 2:8-9).

front: What is the role of the Holy Spirit in salvation?
back: The Spirit works in believers, guiding them to live holy lives and strengthening their faith.

front: What is atonement?
back: Restoring the relationship between people and God through Jesus' death and resurrection — "at-one-ment".

front: Give a quotation about atonement.
back: "He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world" (1 John 2:2).

front: How does the "Jesus bridge" illustrate salvation?
back: Sin creates a gap between sinful people and a holy God. Jesus' death on the cross bridges the gap so people can be with God.

front: How do Christians remember Jesus' sacrifice today?
back: In the Eucharist (Holy Communion), sharing bread and wine as Jesus did at the Last Supper.

front: The six articles of faith in Sunni Islam.
back: Tawhid, angels, holy books, prophethood, Day of Judgement, supremacy of God's will.
items: The Day of Judgement / life after death

front: The five roots of Usul ad-Din in Shi'a Islam.
back: Tawhid, Adalat (justice), prophethood, the imamate, resurrection and judgement.
items: Mi'ad — the Day of Judgement and resurrection

front: Two similarities and two differences: six articles vs five roots.
back: Similar: both include Tawhid and prophethood (and the Day of Judgement). Different: only Sunni lists angels and holy books; only Shi'a lists Adalat (God's justice) and the imamate.

front: Why did Islam split into Sunni and Shi'a?
back: A dispute after Muhammad's death about who should lead the Muslims.

front: What is Tawhid?
back: The oneness and unity of God — the most important belief in Islam.

front: Quote Surah 112 on Tawhid.
back: "Say, He is God the One, God the eternal. He begot no one nor was He begotten. No one is comparable to Him."

front: What are the words of the Shahadah?
back: "There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah."

front: What is shirk?
back: Associating anything with God or treating it as equal to God — the worst sin in Islam.

front: Immanent vs transcendent.
back: Immanent: God is close to and involved in the world. Transcendent: God is beyond and outside the world. Muslims believe God is both.

front: What is Adalat?
back: The justice of God — God is fair and judges actions, rewarding good and punishing evil. One of the Shi'a five roots.

front: Five qualities of God in Islam.
back: Omnipotent, beneficent, merciful, fair, just.
items: Merciful — forgives those who are truly sorry
Just — judges and rewards or punishes

front: What are angels in Islam?
back: Spiritual beings made by God from light, who have no free will and act as God's messengers.

front: What is the role of Jibril?
back: The angel who brought God's messages to the prophets — above all, the Qur'an to Muhammad, starting on the Night of Power.

front: What is the role of Mika'il?
back: The angel of mercy: rewards righteous people and sends rain to nourish the earth.

front: Which angel will blow the trumpet on the Day of Judgement?
back: Israfil.

front: What is predestination (al-Qadr)?
back: The idea that God knows or decides everything that will happen in the universe.

front: Sunni vs Shi'a views on predestination.
back: Sunni: God has already decided everything (the Book of Decrees), though humans are still responsible. Shi'a: God knows what will happen but does not decide it — humans have free will.

front: Give a Qur'an quotation on predestination.
back: "Only what God has decreed will happen to us" (Qur'an 9:51).

front: How does predestination link to the Day of Judgement?
back: If humans had no free will it would be unfair to judge them. So Muslims hold that people are still responsible and accountable for their choices.

front: What is Akhirah?
back: Everlasting life after death.

front: What is barzakh?
back: The state of waiting ("barrier") between death and the Day of Judgement.

front: Give a Qur'an quotation about accountability on the Day of Judgement.
back: "Whoever has done an atom's weight of good will see it" (Qur'an 99:7).

front: Jannah vs Jahannam.
back: Jannah: paradise, a garden of happiness, "a reward for what they used to do" (56:24). Jahannam: hell, fire and torment for those who reject God or do evil.

front: What is Risalah?
back: Prophethood — the communication between God and humans through prophets.

front: How many prophets are there believed to be, and how many are named in the Qur'an?
back: About 124,000; 25 are named in the Qur'an.

front: Why is Adam important in Islam?
back: The first man and first prophet, created by God from clay; the father of the human race. He was tempted by Iblis but repented and was forgiven.

front: Why is Ibrahim important in Islam?
back: He rejected idols and taught one God, rebuilt the Ka'aba, and was willing to sacrifice his son for God — remembered at Id-ul-Adha and on Hajj.

front: What does "Seal of the Prophets" mean?
back: Muhammad is the final prophet — there will be none after him (Qur'an 33:40).

front: What happened on the Night of Power?
back: In 610 CE, aged 40, Muhammad received the first revelation of the Qur'an from Jibril on Mount Hira.

front: The five holy books and who received each.
back: Qur'an — Muhammad; Tawrat — Musa; Zabur — Dawud; Injil — Isa; Sahifah — Ibrahim.

front: Why is the Qur'an the highest authority for Muslims?
back: It is God's final, complete and unchanged word, revealed to Muhammad through Jibril. "This is the Scripture in which there is no doubt" (Qur'an 2:2).

front: Why do the earlier holy books not carry the same authority as the Qur'an?
back: They were lost (the Sahifah) or their texts were changed over time.

front: What is a hafiz?
back: Someone who has learned the whole Qur'an by heart.

front: What is the imamate?
back: In Shi'a Islam, the divine appointment of the imams — Ali and his descendants — to lead the Muslim community.

front: Who did Sunni and Shi'a Muslims accept as Muhammad's successor?
back: Sunni: Abu Bakr, Muhammad's father-in-law, then Umar, Uthman and Ali as caliphs. Shi'a: Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, chosen by Muhammad, then his descendants as imams.

front: Why do Shi'a Muslims follow the twelve imams?
back: They were Muhammad's descendants through Ali and Fatimah, chosen by God, infallible, and guard the true meaning of the Qur'an.
hint: The school sheet says they were not family. They were.

front: Two contrasting Christian views on homosexuality.
back: Catholic: the orientation is not sinful but sexual acts are (some cite Leviticus 18:22). Liberal Christians (e.g. Quakers, Methodists): loving same-sex relationships are equal and they will marry same-sex couples.

front: What is the main Muslim view on homosexuality?
back: Most Muslims believe the Qur'an and hadith teach homosexual acts are against God's will; the only permitted sexual relationship is between husband and wife.

front: Christian views on sex before marriage.
back: Catholic and most Christians: wrong — sex belongs in marriage. Some liberal Christians: acceptable in a loving, committed relationship, especially if the couple plan to marry.

front: Why do almost all Christians believe adultery is wrong?
back: It breaks the wedding vows made before God and the commandment "You shall not commit adultery" (Exodus 20:14).

front: What is zina?
back: Sexual activity outside marriage — including sex before marriage and adultery — forbidden in Islam.

front: Give a Qur'an quotation on adultery.
back: "Do not go anywhere near adultery: it is an outrage and an evil path" (Qur'an 17:32).

front: Catholic vs Church of England on contraception.
back: Catholic: only natural methods — sex is for making life and expressing love, which must not be separated. Church of England: artificial contraception is fine for responsible family planning.

front: What do most Muslims believe about contraception?
back: It is acceptable within marriage to space children or protect the mother's health, but not to avoid having children altogether.

front: Christian purposes of marriage.
back: Companionship, a loving sexual relationship, having children, bringing them up in the faith.
items: Having children — "be fruitful and increase in number"
Bringing children up in the Christian faith

front: Give a hadith about marriage.
back: "There is no institution in Islam more beloved to God than marriage." Also: a man who marries completes half his religion.

front: What is cohabitation?
back: A couple living together without being married.

front: Two contrasting religious views on cohabitation.
back: Catholic Church and Islam: wrong — sex belongs only in marriage. Many Protestant Christians: acceptable if the couple are committed, often as a step towards marriage.

front: Why did many Christians oppose same-sex marriage becoming legal?
back: Not because they opposed equal rights, but because they believe marriage was set by God as one man and one woman, and the law changed that.

front: What does Jesus teach about divorce in Mark 10:11?
back: "Anyone who divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery against her."

front: Catholic vs Church of England on divorce.
back: Catholic: no divorce — marriage is a permanent sacrament; an annulment may say it was never valid. Church of England: divorce allowed, and remarriage in church at the vicar's discretion.

front: What is an annulment?
back: A Catholic Church ruling that a marriage was never valid.

front: Describe the Muslim process of divorce.
back: Allowed as a last resort. The husband declares talaq; a three-month waiting period (iddah) follows, to allow reconciliation and check for pregnancy. A woman can seek divorce through a court.

front: Give a hadith about divorce.
back: "Of all lawful things, divorce is the most hated by God."

front: Sanctity of vows vs compassion — two ethical arguments on divorce.
back: Sanctity of vows: promises made before God are sacred — "What God has joined together, let no one separate" (Mark 10:9). Compassion: forcing someone to stay in an abusive or loveless marriage causes harm, so divorce can be the loving choice.

front: What is a nuclear family?
back: A couple and their children.

front: What is an extended family?
back: A family that includes grandparents and other relatives as well as parents and children.

front: Give a Qur'an quotation about caring for parents.
back: "Your Lord has commanded that you should worship none but Him, and be kind to your parents" (Qur'an 17:23).

front: Four purposes of the family.
back: Procreation, stability, protecting children, educating children in a faith.
items: Stability — for the couple and for society

front: Give a Bible teaching about children and parents.
back: "Honour your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12) — one of the Ten Commandments.

front: What is polygamy?
back: Having more than one wife or husband at the same time. Illegal in the UK.

front: What does Islam teach about polygamy?
back: A man may have up to four wives, but only if he can treat them equally — "if you fear you cannot be equitable, then marry only one" (Qur'an 4:3).

front: Two Christian views on same-sex parents.
back: Catholic and some others: a child needs a mother and a father as role models. Liberal Christians: a loving, stable home is what matters.

front: Give a Bible teaching on gender equality.
back: "There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28).

front: Catholic vs Church of England on women priests.
back: Catholic: only men, because Jesus' apostles were men. Church of England: women priests since 1994 and bishops since 2014 — Paul sent Phoebe as a church representative.

front: What does Islam teach about the equality of men and women?
back: They were created from a single soul and are spiritually equal, with equal rewards from God (Qur'an 33:35), though traditionally with different roles.

front: Prejudice vs discrimination.
back: Prejudice: unfairly judging someone (an attitude). Discrimination: acting against someone because of that prejudice (an action).

front: Which UK law made gender discrimination illegal?
back: The Sex Discrimination Act 1975.

front: What is reconciliation?
back: Restoring friendly relations after conflict or disagreement.

front: What is justice?
back: Bringing about what is right and fair, according to the law, or making up for a wrong.

front: How many times did Jesus say to forgive?
back: "Seventy times seven" (Matthew 18:22) — in other words, without limit.

front: Give a Christian example of reconciliation work.
back: The Community of the Cross of Nails, based at Coventry Cathedral (bombed in 1940), which works for reconciliation around the world.

front: Give a Qur'an quotation on reconciliation or forgiveness.
back: "When aggressive people address them, they reply with words of peace" (Qur'an 25:63). Or: "anyone who forgives and puts things right will have his reward from God" (42:40).

front: Christian views on violent protest.
back: Most: only peaceful protest — "turn the other cheek"; e.g. Martin Luther King Jr. A few: "righteous anger" can be justified, as Jesus overturned the tables in the Temple.

front: What is terrorism?
back: The unlawful use of violence, usually against innocent civilians, to achieve a political goal.

front: Give a Qur'an quotation against terrorism.
back: "Do not take life, which God has made sacred" (Qur'an 17:33). Or "whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had killed all mankind" (5:32).

front: Three reasons for war.
back: Greed, self-defence, retaliation.
items: Greed — selfish desire for land, resources or power
Retaliation — hitting back after being harmed

front: What does 1 Timothy 6:10 say about greed?
back: "The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil."
hint: Not "money is the root of all evil".

front: How did Jesus change the teaching "eye for eye"?
back: "If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to them the other cheek also" (Matthew 5:39) — no retaliation.

front: The conditions for a just war.
back: Just cause, proper authority, right intention, last resort, reasonable chance of success, proportionality.
items: Proportionality — no more force than needed; civilians not targeted

front: Who developed the Christian just war theory?
back: St Augustine (4th–5th century), developed by Thomas Aquinas (13th century). It is not in the Bible.

front: Greater jihad vs lesser jihad.
back: Greater jihad: the inner struggle to live as a good Muslim — the more important. Lesser jihad: the outward struggle to defend Islam, which can include holy war.

front: When can a war NOT be called jihad?
back: If it is for political reasons, to force conversion, to gain land, puts women and children at risk, or destroys homes, places of worship, crops or trees.
items: Fought for political reasons or to gain territory
To force people to convert to Islam
Puts women, children or civilians at risk
Destroys homes or places of worship

front: When did the Crusades take place?
back: The 11th to 13th centuries — Christians fought Muslims for control of Jerusalem.

front: What is pacifism?
back: The belief that war and violence can never be justified, even in self-defence.

front: Which Christian denomination is pacifist, and what did it do in the world wars?
back: The Quakers (Society of Friends). They ran the Friends' Ambulance Unit.

front: Why is Islam not a pacifist religion?
back: Lesser jihad can be a duty: "Fighting has been ordained for you, though it is hard for you" (Qur'an 2:216). But if the enemy offers peace, Muslims must accept (8:61).

front: Is religion a cause of war today? One point each way.
back: Yes: extremist groups such as Islamic State claim religious reasons for violence. No: most conflicts are mainly about land, power or resources, and religious teachings promote peace.

front: What is nuclear deterrence?
back: Holding nuclear weapons so that other countries will not dare attack you.

front: Two Christian views on nuclear weapons.
back: Against: they break "You shall not murder" and fail proportionality; Pope Francis said even possessing them is immoral. For deterrence: some accept keeping them to keep the peace, but never using them.

front: Three types of weapon of mass destruction.
back: Nuclear, chemical, biological.
items: Nuclear — nuclear reaction, devastating huge areas

front: Why do most Muslims oppose WMDs?
back: They kill civilians and damage the environment, breaking the limits of war: "do not overstep the limits" (Qur'an 2:190).

front: Name a religious peacemaker and what they did.
back: Archbishop Desmond Tutu led South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Or Imam Ashafa and Pastor Wuye founded the Interfaith Mediation Centre in Nigeria.

front: Ways religious believers can work for peace.
back: Prayer, peaceful protest, campaigning, interfaith dialogue, supporting peace and aid charities.

front: How does Islamic Relief help victims of war?
back: Emergency aid in disasters and war, plus long-term help to rebuild communities — for anyone regardless of race, politics, gender or belief. "Whoever saves a life, it is as if he saved the lives of all mankind" (Qur'an 5:32).

front: How does Christian Aid help victims of war?
back: Works to end poverty, including helping refugees from war. Slogan: "We believe in life before death". Motivated by "love your neighbour" and the Good Samaritan.

front: What is a refugee?
back: Someone forced to leave their country because of war or persecution.
